item.title: We Are Adding Malaika Gray and Marioo’s New Single “My Fever” Straight to Our Playlist
item.description: If you’ve ever fallen so hard for someone that your whole world changes, Malaika Gray and Marioo ’s new track is going to speak directly to your heart. The duo have come together for “ My Fever ,” a beautiful track that captures the exact feeling of realizing you are in deep. It speaks to that moment when someone becomes your favourite person, and the one you want next to you through everything life throws at you. Calling the song “My Fever” says everything about the intensity of this love. Whenever these two are together, the energy is completely off the charts. It is about being totally taken with someone in the best possible way. Beyond all that energy, the song is built on love. It is not just about physical attraction. It focuses on tenderness, showing up for each other, and that clear feeling of knowing you have found your person. “My Fever” celebrates the beautiful experience of loving someone deeply that they become part of your daily life. item.title: “The Legacy Continues”: 2Baba Announces New Album ‘Oldest Young Man’
item.description: 2Baba wearing a hooded black pleated drape and sunglasses to announce his studio album, Oldest Young Man. Afrobeats icon 2Baba is officially returning with a full-length body of work, and November 27 is the date to mark in your calendars! The legendary singer and songwriter—formerly known as 2Face Idibia —took to Instagram to announce his upcoming studio album, titled Oldest Young Man. Taking to social media to share the exciting release date, the Afropop veteran captioned his post: The legacy continues. OLDEST YOUNG MAN drops 27.11.26. Timeless music, no expiration date. The announcement marks a huge moment for African music fans. Oldest Young Man is 2Baba’s first studio album in over six years, following his critically acclaimed 2020 project, Warriors , which featured heavyweights like Burna Boy , Wizkid , and Olamide . While he hasn’t dropped a full-length album since then, the Nigerian music pioneer has remained active with steady releases, most recently dropping singles like “ Mental ” in September 2026 and “ Ifesinachi ” earlier in the year. With over two decades at the top of the game—stretching from his days with Plantashun Boiz to solo anthems like “ African Queen “—the legend is set to prove once again why his sound stands the test of time. item.title: Funke Akindele, Waje & Shoday’s London Looks Belong in Our Style Notes | See Photos
item.description: Funke Akindele, Shoday, and Waje smiling during their London promotional walk ahead of The Four UK premiere. Upon seeing these photos of Funke Akindele , Shoday and Waje , we had no choice but to pull out our notes, ready for some styling lessons. Did you see how they coordinated their looks for their London outing? Funke and Waje gave us matching buba and iro sets with colourful floral details, while Shoday arrived with a custom embroidered blazer that made its own case for a place in our style notes. The trio were in the UK for the promotional campaign of The Four: No One Fights Alone , and the outing came with another exciting update. Funke Akindele Network and FilmOne Entertainment have announced that the film will have its UK premiere on 29 November at ODEON Luxe Leicester Square in London, ahead of its worldwide cinema release on 11 December. Now, if you’re wondering how Funke and Waje managed to wear matching outfits without looking identical, the answer is in the details. Both looks started with off-white textured cotton, but the floral appliqués gave each one a distinct finish. Funke’s outfit features crimson-red roses with spiral stitching across the bodice and bell sleeves, while yellow sunflowers and leafy green stems run down her wrapper. She completed the look with a golden-yellow head wrap, layered gold necklaces, a broad cuff bracelet and metallic red platform sandals. Funke Akindele Buba and Iro Outfit for The Four London Promo Waje went for lavender roses across the neckline and sleeves of her blouse, with large green floral appliqués decorating the hem of her wrapper. She kept the colour story going with a matching lavender-trimmed scarf, a gold necklace accented with turquoise stones, coordinating earrings and multi-coloured platform heels. Same base colour, different floral story. We love that. Waje outdoors in London promoting The Four: No One Fights Alone in a lavender floral buba and iro set. And Shoday? He clearly had no plans to be the odd one out. His single-breasted blazer featured bold chevron embroidery in turquoise, yellow, red and blue, worn over a beige mesh-knit top and cream wide-leg trousers. Stacked silver Cuban-link chains and dark dress shoes completed the look, giving the colourful jacket room to do its thing. Shoday in a custom geometric chevron-embroidered blazer during The Four promotional tour in London. With the fashion notes taken, we’re also looking forward to seeing what the cast has in store for the London premiere. The Four: No One Fights Alone features Funke Akindele, Waje, Chioma Akpotha, Bisola Aiyeola, Richard Mofe-Damijo, Lateef Adedimeji, Timini Egbuson and Uzor Arukwe, among others. The film premieres at ODEON Luxe Leicester Square on 29 November before its global cinema release on 11 December. item.title: Ejiro Amos Tafiri Unveils REVERIE, Its Spring/Summer 2027 Collection, Celebrating Reinvention in African Luxury
item.description: Ejiro Amos Tafiri , a Pan-African luxury fashion house founded in Lagos in 2010, has unveiled REVERIE, its Spring/Summer 2027 (SS27) collection, at an exclusive private showcase in Lagos on Sunday, October 25, 2026, held alongside Lagos Fashion Week. The showcase brought together distinguished guests, fashion industry leaders, patrons and representatives of the British Council Nigeria, including chef and media personality Hilda Baci, for a presentation of the house’s latest collection. REVERIE explores renewal and reinvention through contemporary African luxury. Bringing together expressive silhouettes, intricate craftsmanship and a refined colour palette, the collection presents a visual statement that celebrates the evolving language of African fashion. Through considered design and craftsmanship, REVERIE reflects the house’s continued exploration of contemporary African aesthetics, presenting pieces that balance creative expression with the distinctive design sensibility for which Ejiro Amos Tafiri is known. Founded by designer Ejiro Amos Tafiri, known for her signature Drapes, the fashion house has spent 16 years developing a distinctive identity within the luxury fashion landscape. Its design language is characterized by expressive drapery, fluid tailoring and the thoughtful use of indigenous textiles, bringing African craftsmanship into contemporary fashion. The Lagos unveiling followed the third edition of Fashioning a Legacy: Leaving a Mark in Time, held on Saturday, October 24, 2026, at the British Council in Ikoyi, Lagos. The conference brought together designers, stylists, retail professionals and emerging creatives to discuss building sustainable careers and creating lasting impact within the fashion industry. Together, the events reflect Ejiro Amos Tafiri’s continued engagement with the broader creative ecosystem, connecting fashion, education, craftsmanship and the development of emerging talent. The REVERIE presentation forms part of the house’s 16-year milestone and will be followed by an exclusive showcase in Abuja on November 21, 2026. The forthcoming event will bring together members of the diplomatic community, government officials, fashion patrons and invited guests for a further presentation of the house’s work. As Ejiro Amos Tafiri looks towards its next chapter, REVERIE embodies an ongoing exploration of renewal and reinvention, reinforcing the house’s commitment to advancing contemporary African luxury through expressive design and intricate craftsmanship. Students competed for individual honours and school points while gaining valuable experience in a structured, multi-sport environment. The competition also welcomed sporting stakeholders and scouts, reinforcing the wider ambition of the Pan-African School Games: to give young athletes a platform where their abilities can be demonstrated, recognized and developed. Day Two: Athletics Puts Young Athletes to the Test Athletics took centre stage on the second day, with track and field events testing the speed, strength, coordination and technique of the young competitors. Athletes competed in running, jumping and throwing events, earning points for their schools as the standings developed. The athletics programme added another dimension to the Games, highlighting the variety of talent within the participating schools and the value of giving young athletes opportunities to develop through competition. Day Three: Football and the Closing Ceremony Football completed the sporting programme on the final day, with school teams competing for their last honours across the age categories. The matches brought the three-day competition to its conclusion, with the closing ceremony recognizing the achievements of the participating schools and their athletes. One of the major highlights was the presentation of a brand-new school bus to Grange School, sponsored by Mikano Changan Motors . The prize recognised Grange School’s overall victories in the U-13 and U-15 categories and represented a significant reward for the school’s performance across the Games. The presentation was a memorable part of the closing ceremony, giving the competition a lasting highlight beyond the medals and results. Recognizing the Schools and Their Achievements The final results reflected strong performances across swimming, athletics and football. Grange School secured the overall titles in the U-13 and U-15 categories, while St. Saviour’s School, Ikoyi, won the overall U-11 title. Grange School’s performances across the U13 category earned it the overall prize sponsored by Mikano Changan Motors. St. Saviour’s School’s success in the U-11 category also highlighted the competitive strength of the younger athletes. The results reflected the contributions of students across the participating schools, many of whom competed in multiple events and disciplines. They also reinforced the importance of consistent preparation, teamwork and participation in structured sporting activities. School representatives celebrate their achievements at the Pan-African School Games 2026 closing ceremony. Scouts and Opportunities Beyond Competition A particularly important aspect of the 2026 Games was the presence of scouts, brought to the event by Plumptre Advisory . Their attendance strengthened the talent-identification dimension of the competition, creating opportunities for promising young athletes to be observed in a competitive setting. For students with sporting potential, being seen by relevant stakeholders can be an important step in exploring future development opportunities. The involvement of Plumptre Advisory also reflects the broader ambition of the Pan-African School Games to connect school sport with educational and developmental pathways. Through its links with international schools and its work around educational opportunities, Plumptre Advisory contributes to conversations about how young people can pursue their academic goals while continuing to develop their sporting abilities. item.description: From November 5 to 8, 2026 , Lagos will become the epicenter of African creativity as Afrique Femme brings the 6th edition of the Brunch des AfricanWoman2.0 to CANEX WKND 2026 at the iconic Wole Soyinka Centre for Culture & Creative Arts. Organized by Afreximbank in collaboration with the African Union and the AfCFTA Secretariat, Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX WKND) is Africa’s premier event celebrating the continent’s creative and cultural industries. Under the overarching theme “One People, United in Culture, Creating for the World: From FESTAC ’77 to CANEX ’27,” this year’s gathering will connect thousands of creative entrepreneurs, investors, policymakers, and cultural icons from across Global Africa and the diaspora. Attendees will experience exclusive collections from celebrated brands including Makeda by AYA Konan ,, KUMI , KWELAKU , and Galipette Atelier , highlighting the richness, craftsmanship, and global potential of Francophone fashion. One retraining program they discussed moved 7,200 of 8,000 university graduates into tech jobs. The difference between charity and philanthropy, they said, is helping people help themselves. The day also asked hard questions about who belongs. A panel on migration, moderated by Dr Ndidi Okonkwo Nwuneli of Wealth4Impact, took on xenophobia, with Lungi Morrison of IFé Consulting and Dr Mbongiseni Buthelezi of the Nelson Mandela Foundation arguing that South Africa’s healing after apartheid was never completed. Dr. Nwuneli ended with a hope that every African child can say, “I am proudly African.” The conversation then looked beyond the continent. The plenary on proximate solutions from the Global South, moderated by Serah Malaba of Tiko, asked what Africa can learn from proximate leaders and funders across the Global South and how trust-based funding reaches those closest to the problem. The panel, which included Amadou Mbodj of Fundación Avina and Divya Patel, CEO of the Ishk Tolaram Foundation, urged funders to pool resources, listen to organizations’ own models, and never ask a partner to compromise its core values. Mbodj warned that funding water, security, and economic decline separately limits impact. Alongside the plenaries, Imagination Sessions ran through the day on themes including family capital, corporate giving, and alternative funding. In the evening, satellite dinners held in partnership with Skoll, the Imago Dei Fund, and African collaboratives carried the conversations into the night. The question of who tells Africa’s story took center stage next. Chude Jideonwo, Founder of Joy, Inc., told delegates that “confident power does not wait for approval” and that Africa needs “main character energy.” In the plenary on narratives and soft power, moderated by Vimbai Masiyiwa of Batoka Africa, he said philanthropy has fed the deficit narrative about Africa, though not out of malice, and urged funders to give creators real creative freedom. “Storytelling is not an add-on,” he said. “It is what we do at the start.” Julia Quinn, author of the Bridgerton series and a Goodwill Ambassador and Board Member of Landesa, spoke about her wish for women to “own the pond,” and Matthew Ilube, Trustee of the African Gifted Foundation, urged decision makers to “have young people in mind.” Parallel Bridge Sessions ran through the day. The Bridge Sessions looked at education and AI, gender justice and technology, film and the creative economy, and health and climate. In the AI plenary, moderated by Nyimpini Mabunda, panelists agreed the technology can ease due diligence but should not replace human judgment. Toyin Akinniyi of Luminate warned that using AI to decide who gets funded “will not work,” and Janade du Plessis of Launch Africa Ventures called on philanthropists to “invest in the plumbing” and push for policy and regulation. Nyimpini offered a note of humility: “If anyone tells you they are an expert in AI, they are lying; we are all figuring it out.” The closing keynote on legacy paired Nomfundo Ncuphuka, a Masters of African Philanthropy candidate at Wits Business School and CAPSI, with Dr. Judy Dlamini, Founder and Chairperson of the Female Academic Leaders Fellowship. We have to imagine it with them.” Unmuted: Your Turn to Give A fireside session closed the program, and then the conference turned from conversation to action. Through StartPoint, APF launched the Unmuted Campaign, which aims to raise $1 million for African-led organizations. Launching it, APF Board Member Swithin Munyantwali, Co-Founder of the International Law Institute African Centre for Legal Excellence, spoke about why visibility and support matter for the people already making change in their communities. The campaign will start in Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa. The organizations supported through Unmuted are African-led NGOs that have been trained, vetted, and confirmed by an independent advisory committee, so every donor can give knowing their money is going to committed, credible work. The night ended with delegates motivated to do more than they are already doing. That energy does not have to stay in Cape Town. item.description: The Pepsi Agba Baller Promo by Seven-Up Bottling Company (SBC) has launched with over 720 winners, including 4 millionaires, emerging in the first live draws for the ₦800 million reward pool across selected participating regions. The promotion officially commenced on October 28, 2026 and began its live prize draws on November 2, giving eligible consumers the opportunity to win cash prizes while enjoying their favourite SBC beverages. The promotion is running across Lagos, Ogun, Oyo, Kwara, Osun, Ekiti, Kogi, Niger and Ondo states offering consumers an opportunity to win everyday until January 3, 2027. With ₦800 million in total rewards, the Pepsi Agba Baller promo features a winner every minute from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. daily, four ₦1 million winners every day, and a ₦10 million mega jackpot winner every Sunday. The first set of winners includes Oluwatoyin , Oreofe and Damilola from Lagos, and Adeniyi from Ogun State, who each won ₦1 million on the opening day of the draws. Speaking on the promotion , Yewande Ade-Alao , Marketing Manager at SBC, said, “At Seven-Up Bottling Company, we are always looking for ways to make our consumers’ experiences more rewarding. With the Pepsi Agba Baller Promo, consumers can win cash prizes while enjoying the beverages they love. We are excited to see consumers already winning, and we look forward to rewarding many more participants in the promotion.” The Pepsi Agba Baller Promo adds excitement to the festive season, rewarding consumer loyalty and giving eligible consumers a reason to look out for the distinctive yellow covers on Pepsi, 7UP, Mirinda, Teem and other Seven-Up Bottling Company products. To participate, consumers need to purchase eligible products from SBC with the yellow cover to get the unique code printed underneath. Participants can then enter the draw by dialing or scanning the QR code on the bottles and promotional materials for a chance to win a share of the ₦800 million prize pool. Consumers can check the winners’ list and verify their winnings on the official campaign website . To ensure consumer protection, winners are contacted through the designated promotion number, 0700 134 1104, and will receive a confirmation SMS. For additional assistance or enquiries, please contact Seven-Up Bottling Company’s dedicated consumer support lines: 0805 690 0900 and 0806 690 0900. Africans are leveraging AI for business, education and more, but as AI continues to develop and expand rapidly, it is crucial for us to use it on a bigger scale, ensuring collective development and an equitable future for all. This makes the Goalkeepers 2026 event in Dakar particularly significant. item.title: LagosFashionWeek2026: Personal Style Is Alive and Well – Just Ask Ifeoma Odogwu
item.description: From runway shows to intimate presentations and the week’s most stylish gatherings, the fashion editor and creative consultant made a case for directional dressing with oodles of personality. Ifeoma Odogwu , better known as Hyperfashun , is easily one of the best dressed women in Lagos, and arguably on the continent and per usual her Lagos Fashion Week style is peerless. A familiar face in Nigeria’s fashion industry, the former Genevieve Magazine fashion editor, stylist to stars such as Toke Makinwa and more, the creative consultant has spent years working with designers, discovering emerging talent and helping shape the visual language of Nigerian fashion. So, naturally, when Lagos Fashion Week comes around, we’re just as interested in what she’s wearing as we are in what she’s watching. From the bustling Lagos Fashion Week tents at Federal Palace Hotel to a packed calendar of offsite presentations and fashion events across the city, Odogwu embraced the occasion with a wardrobe that made getting dressed part of the experience. At the tents, she joined the fashion crowd for presentations by Y’Wande , NYA The Label , E.S.O by Liman and FIA Factory , taking in some of the exciting design talent shaping the season. But as anyone familiar with Lagos Fashion Week knows, the shows have evolved. Some of the week’s most interesting moments happen elsewhere, and Odogwu’s itinerary reflected just how much the city’s fashion calendar has expanded. She made the rounds at presentations by Jewel Jemila , The Ladymaker, Rendoll, Kilentar, Onalaja and Orange Culture , and made time for the social side of fashion week, too, including the Made By Us pop-up at Melrose Loft and Tiffany Amber’s Breakfast Club. What makes Odogwu particularly interesting to watch is the perspective she brings to personal style. As someone whose career has been built around fashion imagery, designers and creative expression, her wardrobe offers another way of engaging with the industry she’s helped champion. Ifeoma has a certain clarity in her style and an unmatched point of view, something that’s often lacking in the sameness of our Instagram-driven world. Her style reminds us that what makes personal style compelling is individuality, curiosity and a willingness to have fun with fashion. item.title: For the Girls, For Our Health: The Active Circle x Zephans & Co. Celebrate Breast Cancer Awareness Month With The Girls’ Club
item.description: Breast Cancer Awareness Month ended on the most vibrant, empowering note in Lagos! The Active Circle , powered by contemporary fashion brand Zephans & Co. , brought together fabulous women from all walks of life for The Girls’ Club – a dreamy, pink-hued wellness wonderland created to celebrate womanhood while championing critical conversations around breast health. Dr. Salako unpacked the importance of early detection, self-examinations, and practical steps for proactive health, making the conversation feel personal, approachable, and empowering. Chisom Okuguni, Convener of The Active Circle, shared that the initiative was designed to equip women with the knowledge and community support needed to prioritize their well-being every single day. The wellness morning provided an opportunity for the ladies to interact and share experiences, connect on a deeper level, all while learning to care for their breast health. item.title: How the New Tax Stamp Could Show Up in Everyday Life
item.description: We’ve all been there: planning a weekend dinner with friends, throwing a birthday bash, or just kicking back at home with a few favourite treats. Drinks and refreshments are basically a staple of these moments. But have you ever stopped to think about how behind-the-scenes government policies end up changing the price tags on those items? With the Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) rolling out its new excise stamp policy in January 2026, that question is at the forefront, especially for brands that make things like alcohol, tobacco, and sugar-sweetened beverages. Honestly, nobody’s really stressing over the policy itself. What people care about is the ripple effect: how companies handle the new regulation and whether those adjustments will make our favourite items more expensive on the shelf. When Business Meets Your Wallet Behind every product is a mountain of decisions from packaging and distribution to compliance and production. Most of the time, we never see this happening, but it plays a huge role in how items are priced. When new regulations bring extra costs, companies find themselves at a crossroads. Some choose to absorb the blow internally to keep customers happy, while others might tweak their prices. It really comes down to the specific brand, the market, and how heavy the financial lift is. For everyday shoppers, that’s usually the moment a boring policy talk suddenly feels very real. What Does This Mean for How We Spend ? The change probably won’t hit overnight, and it might not even be dramatic. But over time, small shifts in everyday prices can change how we shop. You might find yourself comparing brands a bit more closely, hunting for promos and discounts, or rethinking how much cash you drop on certain treats. Brands, meanwhile, are caught in a tricky balancing act: keeping loyal customers without going broke on rising operating costs. Just keep in mind: a new tax stamp doesn’t automatically mean prices are shooting up. It all depends on how companies adapt and whether those extra costs trickle down to us. The Bigger Picture At the end of the day, this is really about finding a middle ground. The government wants solid systems to collect taxes, while businesses need a framework that lets them stay afloat and grow. But come to think of it, the authorities are already equipped with internal tracking solutions, such as electronic invoicing from FIRS alongside the Customs Service’s B’Odogwu digital excise register, rendering physical paper tags largely redundant. Striking that balance matters because business decisions don’t just stay on a spreadsheet. They shape the things we buy, the choices we make, and how we manage our money. Right now, it’s still a bit early to tell what the full impact on consumers will be. But staying clued in on what’s driving the market makes it a whole lot easier to navigate the changes coming our way. I went to the next one.” “Johnny Walka. Why didn’t you simply take a cab? See as you punish yourself on top £20.” “I no bi God na. I no see say na so e go bẹ.” I stood up, stretched and began walking into the waters. “Babe, you wan jump inside water? No koba mẹ o,” she screeched. “Olódò ni e. Jump say wetin happen? Say she save money wey I for pay the therapist?” “Wow, that is awesome. Look how you reframed it already. Instead of you to say you miss your wellbeing session, you said she miss money.” “Isn’t that the truth? She just missed this £50 quid. I will see if I can book with the other Polish woman at my àdúgbò or maybe try that Egyptian guy for acupuncture. Been a long time since I went to him.” “But that Polish woman is more expensive, isn’t she?” Lantana cocked a brow. By now she was standing by the bank of the ocean, still kicking sand. Her morbid aquaphobia meant she wouldn’t dare come in. “Yeah. She charges £50 for 30 minutes. While this babe dey collect same amount for an hour.” “Ọmọ, see levels! Why the margin? Na gold dust she dey use?” “Sebi I tell you say you no get sense? Gold dust how na?” I chuckled and threw water at her. She dodged. “So why the margin? After all, both of them na Asians.” “Lantana. One is Eastern European while one is Asian.” I laughed and waddled further into the ocean. “Besides, one uses her house while the other pays rates and rents.” “Same of same ni. Asian oo, European oo, na the same colour.” “Oh, I forgot you failed Geography at WAEC and managed a pass in History. So why bother explaining it to you?” “Abeg free mẹ. European. Asian, no bi same oyiboo abi dem be black?” She giggled, like a schoolgirl who saw her boyfriend. “So that Egyptian guy now wey be African, you go call am Black sef?” I asked. “Those Arab-wannabes. Na African na–oyibo African.” “Lantana, I take God beg you, mbok. I no get your power. Let me enjoy my quiet time. At least this one is free” “But it won’t serve the same purpose na. That session would have done wonders to your body. Especially after these two days of hard training by Coach L. You can’t even lift your hands above your head from the pain.” “True. I looked forward to enjoying this experience. Especially after recovering from these last weeks. Also, the lymphatic drainage would have helped.” “Dis Obodo–oyinbo sef,” Lantana bristled “Kilode?” I stepped out of the water. “If this was Naija, they for no turn you back na. They would have made allowance for you.” “True. Pata pata, I go pay extra. And that one is even a total experience, not this mockery of a thing they call spa,” I begrudged. “Ah, babe, I miss Naija spa session.” “As in. From the moment you enter, you get the whole star treatment – sauna, steam, exfoliate, bathe before the massage begins. And sometimes pedicure join sef. All for how much na?” “Nne, don’t even go there. The money for that whole experience no still reach this £60 wey dem use for only massage. Let’s not go down to Egypt joo. Comparisons would only spoil this experience now.” “Which one?” She asked, spreading out her arms. “What did you think I was doing inside the water?” I side-eyed her. “Nothing na. Dem dey ask mamiwota wetin she dey do for her house?” She moved farther back as I stepped closer. “So now I don turn mamiwota because I come seaside?” I cackled. “Auntie, everybody know you and water na. It’s still a wonder how you take escape marine kingdom na your momsy head strong pass their own.” “See why I say you no get sense. So because the water is my happy place mean something now?” “No be only happy place. Water na your addiction.” “Na you get your mouth. I only came for cold water therapy, and I am done.” “Cold water therapy inside this cold and wind? You no see say e no normal abi you no get cold water for house?” “That Polish woman taught me the thing when I started going to her for alternative therapy. She said the cold water shock is cool for the system.” “Cold? Before, would it have been hot? A black person like you go dey behave like whitey. Carry cold water dey pour for body. You just carry the poor body fling inside shocking cold water, and you say choice.” “Lantana, I go see you for house. We see the paid bills, but not the hours spent calling doctors, arranging transport, and sitting beside a bed. We see the calm voice saying, “Everything will be fine,” but not the fear or uncertainty behind it. That person everyone calls may also be tired. They may worry about money, struggle with their health, or quietly wonder who would come through for them if they could no longer carry everyone else. Care Has More Than One Currency In Nigeria, many conversations about family responsibility often begin and end with money. Who paid the school fees? Who sent money home? Who handled the rent? Who covered the medical emergency? These questions matter, especially as the cost of living continues to stretch households. But money is only one currency of care. Care can also be time ! The sitting in traffic to pick up someone else’s child; the night spent at the hospital bedside; the regular reminder to an elderly parent to remember their medication. Or listening to the same worry repeatedly because the person telling you has nowhere else to take it. Care can be access ! Advice. Attention. Prayer. Food. Transport. Encouragement. A job referral. A place to stay. A call that says, “I’m outside, come down.” But care comes at a cost, whether small or big. It may cost sleep, emotional energy, peace of mind, or an opportunity that had to be postponed. Black Tax may be one line on the bill, but it is not the whole bill. Much of the cost of care cannot be captured in a bank statement. Strong Is Not a Support System One danger of being known as “the strong one” is that people begin to treat strength as if it were permanent. The calls keep coming because you have always answered. The responsibilities keep growing because you have always managed. And when you finally say, “ I cannot do this right now ,” people may react as though you have changed. This is why many caregivers struggle to ask for help. They have become so used to being the solution that expressing a need can feel like failure. Setting a boundary can feel selfish. Rest can feel irresponsible. But strength is not a support system. A healthy culture of care shouldn’t require one person to stay endlessly available. It should create room for shared responsibility, honest conversations, and for the dependable person to admit, “I need help too.” Care can be beautiful and heavy at the same time. Acknowledging the weight does not make the love less genuine. Care Should Come Full Circle Bringing back our culture of care does not mean Nigerians have stopped caring. We clearly have not. We contribute towards hospital bills for people we have never met. We send food to neighbours. We welcome relatives into our homes. We show up for naming ceremonies, funerals, weddings and emergencies. When formal systems fail, people often become each other’s system. What needs to change is the direction of care. Care should not travel permanently from one person to everyone else. It should be able to return. That means checking on the person who checks on everybody. It means calling without beginning the conversation with, “Please, I need a favour.” It means sharing a responsibility before the person carrying it becomes overwhelmed. It means respecting their boundaries and understanding that “I cannot do it this time” is not the same as “I do not care.” It also means protecting the caregiver’s health, time, finances, and emotional wellbeing. Families can prepare for emergencies together instead of waiting for one person to rescue everyone. Friends can create safe spaces where the strong friend does not always have to perform strength. Workplaces can recognize that employees may also carry significant caregiving responsibilities outside the office. Care becomes stronger when it is shared. Start With a Different Call Think about the last time something went wrong. Whose number did you dial? Now ask yourself a more uncomfortable question: when was the last time you called that person without needing money, advice, access, reassurance, or a solution? Today may be a good day to make a different kind of call. Say, “I don’t need anything. I just wanted to know how you are.” Ask what they are carrying. Offer to take something off their plate. Encourage them to rest. Support their health. Respect their limits. Remind them that being dependable does not mean they must do everything alone. For AXA Mansard, the Culture of Care conversation is grounded in a simple belief: the people who protect others deserve protection too . The brand’s role is not to claim ownership of care. Care already belongs to us. It is to help make invisible care visible and encourage all of us to make it more intentional, reciprocal, and sustainable. So, think about your person. The one whose number everybody knows. The one who always says, “I’ll sort it.” The one who keeps showing up. Name them. Thank them. Protect them. Because the person everyone calls also deserves someone to call. Keep caring for each other. It is the most beautiful form of protection. item.title: Meet Mo Odukoya: Pastor Jimmy Introduces His Wife to The Fountain of Life Church
item.description: Pastor Jimmy Odukoya and Pastor Mo Odukoya pose together following their formal church introduction If you’re a member of The Fountain of Life Church and you were at yesterday’s service, we’re a little jealous. What do you mean you got to witness Pastor Jimmy Odukoya introduce his wife, Mo Jasmine Daniel , to the congregation in person? Yes, right there at the church’s headquarters in Ilupeju, Lagos, the senior pastor had a special person to introduce, and he made sure everyone knew exactly who she was. As she joined him at the altar, he introduced her as Pastor Mo Odukoya , the church’s new first lady, and the congregation welcomed the couple with cheers and applause. Pastor Jimmy Odukoya and his wife, Mo Jasmine Daniel, holding hands during their official introduction at The Fountain of Life Church But before that introduction, Pastor Jimmy had a little story to tell. He spoke about how he had been navigating life alone since becoming the church’s senior pastor, and how he had been searching for someone to share the journey with. He invited Mo to join him, and the two walked up to the altar together, marking the moment with a warm reception from the congregation. Pastor Jimmy Odukoya introduces his wife, Mo Jasmine Daniel, on stage at The Fountain of Life Church in Ilupeju, Lagos For those who know Pastor Jimmy beyond the pulpit, there’s quite a bit to his story. He took over as senior pastor of The Fountain of Life Church in 2023, following the passing of his father, the late Pastor Taiwo Odukoya , who co-founded the ministry with his wife, Pastor Bimbo Odukoya . He is also an actor and musician, and film audiences may recognise him as Oba Ade in the 2022 historical film The Woman King, where he starred alongside Viola Davis . Pastor Jimmy Odukoya and Mo Jasmine Daniel after announcing their marriage to the congregation And now, there’s a new chapter to this story with Mo. Introduced to the congregation as Pastor Mo Odukoya, she is the daughter of Reverend Theophilus and Bolaji Daniel . She also took a moment to address the church, expressing her pleasure and honour at joining the ministry family. The couple also made sure their outfits were in sync for the occasion. Pastor Jimmy wore a structured burnt-orange native outfit with dark detailing on the cuffs and a matching necklace, while Pastor Mo chose a long-sleeved, floor-length dress in orange and copper patterns, finished with a matching clutch and accessories. Thailand Thailand is for the celebrant who wants everything: City energy, beautiful beaches, nightlife, shopping, culture and food. It gives you enough value for money to stop your guests from sending angry voice notes about the budget. Begin in Bangkok. Give everyone time to arrive and recover. Host a rooftop welcome dinner overlooking the city. Then fly to Phuket or Krabi. Book a villa or resort close to the beach. Arrange a private yacht or traditional long-tail boat. Add island hopping and a birthday dinner by the sea. The birthday idea: Bangkok rooftop welcome, Phuket villa stay, private boat celebration and beach dinner. Mexico If you want a birthday everyone will still be talking about five years later, Mexico is for you. Cancún gives you all-inclusive resorts, beach clubs and nightlife. Tulum offers beautiful villas, restaurants and cenotes. Cabo brings dramatic coastline, polished resorts and excellent settings for sunset dinners and boat parties. For a milestone birthday, choose one base rather than trying to cover the entire country. Have a relaxed welcome evening. Settle in. item.title: Loving Itohan, Dear Ajayi & No Fury: 3 Nollywood Films to Watch in Cinemas This November
item.description: Lead stars Nancy Isime and Uzor Arukwe pose in traditional attire for Loving Itohan, arriving in cinemas this November. Photo Credit: Nancy Isime/Instagram This November, we urge you to plan your cinema itinerary well because you are about to be thoroughly entertained by Nollywood’s big-screen offerings. As the end-of-year movie season kicks into high gear, Nigerian filmmakers are serving up a rich mix of emotional romance, deeply moving historical drama, and high-stakes revenge thrillers. Whether you are stepping out for a weekend date night or gathering friends for a popcorn-filled cinematic escape, these three titles promise to make your cinema visits worthwhile. Here are the Nollywood films hitting the big screen this November. Loving Itohan If you are in the mood for a sweeping romantic drama that tests the boundaries of second chances, Loving Itohan should be at the top of your list. Executive produced by Nancy Isime , directed by Orobosa Ikponmwen , and produced by Emmanuel Izuoba , the film brings together a stellar creative team, with Lucas Oluwole capturing the vivid visual landscape as Director of Photography. Nancy Isime and Uzor Arukwe in traditional Edo attire for the romantic Nollywood drama Loving Itohan. item.title: Watch Burna Boy Take Over the NFL Paris Game with a Star-Studded Halftime Show
item.description: Burna Boy backstage at Stade de France wearing a custom 3.PARADIS leather jacket look for the NFL Paris Game. Did you catch Burna Boy at the inaugural NFL Paris Game last weekend? If you missed his halftime performance at the Stade de France in Paris, we have all the details. The Nigerian Grammy Award winner took over the pitch as the Pittsburgh Steelers faced the New Orleans Saints, giving American football fans a taste of West African music. Returning to the 80,000-capacity stadium after his historic solo concert in Paris, Burna Boy opened his set with “ 4 Kampe II ”, his collaboration with French-Haitian singer Joé Dwèt Filé . He moved between English, French and Haitian Creole before welcoming French singer Yseult on stage and moving into some of his biggest hits. The set included “ On the Low ,” “ Ye ” and “ Last Last ,” with a special appearance from French judo champion Teddy Riner adding to the occasion. It was a set that gave fans in the stadium and viewers watching around the world a taste of the Nigerian star’s catalogue. Burna Boy arrives at Stade de France ahead of his halftime show performance at the NFL Paris Game in Paris. Burna Boy also made sure his outfit matched the scale of the performance. He wore custom luxury streetwear, pairing a structured oversized leather jacket with tailored cargo trousers, heavy silver neck chains and dark tinted sunglasses. The NFL Paris Game adds to Burna Boy’s growing list of major international sporting appearances. He has previously performed at the NBA All-Star Game and the UEFA Champions League Final kickoff show, taking African music to audiences well beyond the usual concert stage. The Paris weekend also coincided with the launch of his debut sneaker collaboration with Swiss sportswear brand On, under the No Giant Stands Alone campaign. Away from the stage, he was also spotted backstage catching up with French football star Paul Pogba . item.title: In Photos: Senegal Makes History as the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games Kick Off
item.description: Khaby Lame and Boubou Niang take the stage with a young participant at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games opening ceremony. If you have been keeping an eye on sports and global pop culture, history was made over the weekend in West Africa. Senegal officially kicked off the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games with a spectacular opening ceremony at the 55,000-capacity Stade Abdoulaye Wade in Diamniadio, marking the first time an Olympic event has ever taken place on African soil. Running through to 13 November, the Games are bringing together over 2,600 young athletes aged 14 to 17, competing across 25 sports and 153 medal events. The action spans three vibrant hubs: the historic capital city of Dakar, the modern satellite city of Diamniadio, and the coastal resort area of Saly. Host nation Senegal enters the arena during the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games Parade of Nations. Under the official motto “Africa welcomes, Dakar celebrates”, the opening ceremony turned into a celebration of music, dance, visual arts, and storytelling. Beyond the parade of nations, the night showcased iconic West African talent. Senegalese music legend Baaba Maal led a massive musical tribute alongside Kiné Lam and hip-hop outfit Daara J Family , while Gambian kora virtuoso Sona Jobarteh and social media star Khaby Lame made featured appearances. Massamba Gueye performs during a cultural heritage sequence at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games opening ceremony. Nigeria also took centre stage during the ceremony, with spoken word poet Ibukunoluwa Aramide Ajagbe , popularly known as Ibquake , delivering a live performance surrounded by dancers against a backdrop of stadium lights. Ibquake performing live at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games opening ceremony. The Games feature an exciting, youth-focused sports lineup including 3×3 basketball, futsal, beach volleyball, rugby sevens, breakdancing, street skateboarding, wushu, beach wrestling, table tennis, and archery. Over 200 National Olympic Committees are participating—with strong contingents representing African nations like host nation Senegal, Nigeria,South Africa, Kenya, and Algeria, alongside global delegations including Great Britain, Australia, Germany, Argentina, South Korea, and the United States. With two full weeks of sporting events, cultural showcases, and youth competition ahead, Senegal has set the tone for a historic milestone in African sports and lifestyle history. item.title: Watch Tunde Kelani’s Remastered Agogo Èèwò & Revisit the World of Saworoide
item.description: Official poster for Tunde Kelani’s remastered political classic, “Agogo Èèwò.” If you watched Saworoide , get ready to return to Jogbo. Tunde Kelani ’s political drama Agogo Èèwò (2002), the follow-up to his acclaimed classic, is now available in a newly remastered presentation on TK ÒPÓMÚLÉRÓ’s YouTube channel. Following the fall of military ruler Lagata in Saworoide, the people of Jogbo hope for a new era of peace and prosperity. But the corrupt chiefs have other plans. They install Adebosipo, played by the late veteran actor Dejumo Lewis , as the new king, believing that his background as a retired police officer will make him easy to control as they continue to exploit the kingdom’s treasury. Adebosipo, however, refuses to play along. Determined to protect the people of Jogbo, he demands accountability from the chiefs, setting off a fierce struggle over power, corruption and the future of the kingdom. The conflict reaches a defining moment during a public traditional oath-taking ceremony before the sacred Agogo Èèwò, or Gong of Taboo. Under the custom, anyone who has stolen from the land must confess before the gong sounds seven times, or face the consequences. Written by Professor Akinwunmi Isola and directed by Tunde Kelani, Agogo Èèwò remains a pointed examination of corruption, leadership and traditional systems of accountability. More than two decades after its original release, the film’s return in a remastered version gives audiences another opportunity to revisit the story and its enduring questions about those entrusted with power. The remastered Agogo Èèwò is now streaming on YouTube via TK ÒPÓMÚLÉRÓ. item.title: From Nigeria to Senegal: Ibquake Performs at Historic Dakar 2026 Opening Ceremony
item.description: Ibquake performing live at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games opening ceremony. Senegal came alive yesterday at the opening ceremony of the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, with a vibrant celebration of culture, history and African creativity. Among the performers on stage was Nigeria’s very own Ibukunoluwa Aramide Ajagbe , popularly known as Ibquake , who represented the country with a spoken word performance. The ceremony took place at the Stade Abdoulaye Wade in Diamniadio, just outside Dakar, marking a major moment in sporting history as the first Olympic event to be hosted on African soil. More than 1,100 performers took part in the showcase, which featured music, dance, visual arts and spoken word. Senegalese music legends Baaba Maal and Kiné Lam , music group Daara J Family , Gambian kora musician Sona Jobarteh and social media personality Khaby Lame were among the other names featured. Ibquake on stage with dancers and the lit Olympic cauldron at the Dakar 2026 opening ceremony. Stepping onto the global stage in a structured white gown with a sculptural bodice and braided detailing, Ibquake performed against a backdrop of dancers in feathered and textured costumes. Her verses celebrated African identity, heritage and the possibilities ahead for the continent’s young people. Among the lines she delivered were: “We carry a flame for the African child to look beyond the horizon… We are both root and revolution.” Reflecting on the experience, Ibquake shared a personal message online about what being part of the historic occasion meant to her. She imagined her daughter one day asking when the Olympics first came to Africa, and how she would be able to tell her she was there. She wrote: “My daughter will one day ask me when the first Olympics games happened in Africa. And I’ll answer with speed and alacrity. She’ll ask me how I know… And I’ll say… Because mummy was a part of it.” Ibquake surrounded by dancers during the opening ceremony in Senegal. She went on to describe her life as a testament to God’s goodness and reaffirmed her commitment to telling African stories “Powerfully… Boldly,” adding that Africa will always be great in her eyes. The Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games run from October 31 to November 13, bringing together approximately 2,700 young athletes from 204 National Olympic Committees and the Youth Refugee Olympic Team. Competitions span 25 sports and 153 medal events, with activities taking place in Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly. item.title: ONGA Celebrates Nigeria’s Diverse Food Culture with ‘Cook Your Way With ONGA’ World Food Day Activation
item.description: ONGA , the seasoning brand from Promasidor Nigeria , marked World Food Day with its three-day Cook Your Way With ONGA activation, bringing shoppers together to explore Nigeria’s diverse food cultures and celebrate the individual touches that make every meal their own. Rooted in ONGA’s Taste of Home platform, the campaign recognizes that home is not defined by one recipe or a single way of cooking. item.title: Virgin Atlantic Marks 25 Years in Nigeria – Honours Travel Partners
item.description: L-R: Georgia Mobsby, Senior Manager – Sales Excellence; Anthony Uphill, Vice President Sales; Dave Geer, Chief Commercial Officer; Yann Stirton, Country Manager – West Africa; and Liezl Gericke, Head of International, all of Virgin Atlantic, at an awards evening in Lagos celebrating the airline’s 25 years of operations in Nigeria on 22nd October 2026. British international airline Virgin Atlantic marks 25 years of operations in Nigeria with a special awards evening in Lagos, recognising the travel partners whose contributions have helped sustain and grow the airline’s presence in the country over the past quarter of a century. Held at The George Lagos Hotel on Thursday, 22 October, the event brought together Virgin Atlantic executives, travel industry partners and other stakeholders to commemorate a journey that began in July 2001, when the airline launched its Lagos service with four weekly flights operated by a Boeing 747. Speaking at the celebration, Virgin Atlantic’s Chief Commercial Officer, Dave Geer , described Nigeria as one of the airline’s most important and established markets within its international network, paying tribute to the travel partners, customers, employees and operational partners who have contributed to its success. “Technology will never replace relationships. The trust, local knowledge, and customer understanding represented in this room remain fundamental to our success,” Geer said. He also emphasized the importance of building sustainable partnerships, strengthening customer relationships and ensuring that the airline’s investments continue to support long-term commercial growth. Virgin Atlantic’s Country Manager – West Africa, Yann Stirton , acknowledged the resilience of Nigerian travel partners, particularly through periods of economic uncertainty, currency volatility and restrictions on ticket inventory. Highlighting a significant shift in the airline’s commercial performance, Stirton revealed that ticket sales in Nigeria now generate more revenue for the Lagos route than sales in any other market, including the United Kingdom. “When I arrived in Lagos in September 2023, most of the revenue on this route was sold in the UK. item.title: Can We Talk About Tenicka Boyd’s Lagos Fashion Week Style?
item.description: The American fashion influencer, whose effortlessly polished approach to dressing has earned her a devoted following, has been turning heads in Lagos with a wardrobe that’s equal parts playful and unapologetically sophisticated. And if there’s one thing her appearances have made clear, it’s that Boyd understands the assignment when it comes to fashion week. Scroll through Tenicka Boyd ’s standout Lagos Fashion Week looks below. Tenicka Boyd/Instagram For her Jewel Jemila appearance, Boyd embraced full-on romance in a sweeping fuchsia dress, complete with cascading ruffles and dramatic bell sleeves. Paired with gold jewellery and her signature sleek, centre-parted hair, the look was a masterclass in polished style. Tenicka Boyd/Instagram She switched gears for Beverly Naya ’s Skin Summit experience, opting for a striking black-and-white body-skimming dress with an abstract, zebra-inspired pattern and dramatic fringe detailing. Tenicka Boyd/Instagram But perhaps her most playful look came courtesy of The LadyMaker. Tenicka Boyd/Instagram Boyd paired a sculptural hot-pink puff-sleeve top with a voluminous orange bubble skirt, finishing the look with a purple tasseled handbag and coordinating heels. Tenicka Boyd/Instagram And then there’s this insanely detailed Onalaja burgundy beaded ensemble, a rich, intricately embellished look that traded playful volume for texture and craftsmanship, reinforcing Boyd’s ability to move between different fashion moods without losing her distinct point of view. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Tenicka (@tenickab) Beyond the clothes, Boyd’s Lagos emphasizes the growing visibility of African designers on the global fashion stage. For an influencer whose wardrobe regularly spans international luxury houses and emerging labels, we love that her enthusiasm for Nigerian fashion feels like a natural extension of her personal style. And with looks this good, we’re definitely paying attention. *** Photography: Ayo Makinwa The post Can We Talk About Tenicka Boyd’s Lagos Fashion Week Style? appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. item.title: Money, Fashion & a Little Attitude! Ayra Starr and Theodora’s “Ms. Paper” Video Has It All
item.description: Ayra Starr wears a pink mini dress and side cap in the official “Ms. Paper” music video. Money, fashion, a little attitude, and Ayra Starr ? Oh, we’re definitely watching! The Starrgirl has just dropped the official music video for “ Ms. Paper ,” her collaboration with French rapper Theodora , and the two are having a lot of fun with this one. Taken from Ayra’s album Starrgirl, the fan-favourite track now has a colourful visual to match its playful lyrics. Produced by The Elements, “Ms. Paper” brings together Afropop rhythms and a catchy mix of English and French as Ayra and Theodora sing about making their own money, enjoying their success, and doing things on their own terms. And with a chorus that goes, “Moi, c’est Miss Kitoko ou Miss Paper,” you can already imagine how much fun the music video was going to be. So, what does being Ms. Paper look like? Apparently, it involves plenty of fashion, money, and a little pop-art fun. The video plays around with currency-inspired graphics, retro magazine covers, and custom toy-box packaging, giving Ayra and Theodora their own colourful world to play in. Ayra appears in a pink mini dress with a matching side cap and cowrie shell details before switching things up in a rich blue halter top, bright red hair, and striking face detailing. And there’s still more to enjoy. Between the money-counting scenes, museum-style portrait frames, and choreography, the video keeps finding new ways to bring the song’s playful mood to life. item.title: Google Pay Now Available to Visa Card Holders in Nigeria for Fast, Secure Digital Payments
item.description: Visa , one of the world’s leaders in digital payments, applauds the launch of Google Pay by participating financial institutions in Nigeria, supported through Visa’s partnership with Google . Eligible Visa cardholders of participating financial institutions can now securely add their cards to Google Wallet and make fast, convenient, and secure payments across millions of contactless acceptance points and online merchants. The launch by participating financial institutions marks another significant milestone in Nigeria’s digital payments journey, providing consumers with a simple and secure way to pay using their Android devices. By adding their eligible Visa cards to Google Wallet, users can tap to pay in stores, make purchases online, and enjoy a seamless payment experience across Google’s ecosystem. Google Pay uses tokenization technology to help protect payment information. Instead of storing or sharing a customer’s card number during transactions, a unique digital token is used, providing an additional layer of security while maintaining a fast and convenient checkout experience. As consumer demand for digital-first payment experiences continues to grow, the partnership between Visa and Google, working alongside Nigerian financial institutions, aims to support contactless payment adoption and provide Nigerians with more ways to pay securely wherever Visa contactless payments are accepted. “At Visa, we are committed to advancing the future of payments by delivering innovative, secure, and seamless payment experiences for consumers across Nigeria and beyond . Through our partnership with Google, we are pleased to support our financial institution partners as they bring Google Pay to their cardholders, combining the security of Visa’s global payment network with the convenience consumers increasingly expect in a digital-first world. Helping more people pay with confidence using their mobile devices supports digital commerce, financial inclusion, and the continued growth of Nigeria’s digital economy,” said Andrew Uaboi , Vice President and Cluster Head, Visa West Africa . “We are delighted to bring Google Wallet to Nigeria, a market at the forefront of financial innovation in Africa. item.title: S.E.A CONSULTING Showcases Nigerian Craftsmanship at Design Week Lagos 2026
item.description: At this year’s Design Week Lagos , S.EA.CONSULTING brought its vision to REDESIGN AFRICA to life through an interactive exhibition that invited visitors to touch, listen, explore and connect. Presented at the National Theatre, Lagos, the installation placed local craftsmanship at the centre of a contemporary African living experience. Deep burgundy surfaces, raw tree bark, sculptural textures and a contemporary sofa from S.EA.HOMES created a setting shaped by Nigerian culture and heritage. Finishing materials were served on a dark hardwood table supported by clear acrylic bases, giving the illusion of floating wood. Guests could handle samples and discover the possibilities behind the finished spaces. Wireless headphones offered a choice of music and the founder’s statement, while a digital screen introduced the firm’s services, products, and projects. An in-house photographer captured visitors engaging with the installation, making their presence part of its story. Through this approach, S.EA.CONSULTING made a clear statement: African exhibitions should give local makers, materials and ways of living a central role. Cultural heritage offers a foundation for contemporary design that meets global standards of quality, functionality and execution. The experience connected interior architecture with sourcing, craftsmanship and everyday life, demonstrating how collaboration transforms individual products into spaces with meaning. For S.EA.CONSULTING, showing the world how we live begins with recognising the value of what we make, the stories we carry and the hands that bring our ideas to life. Rooted in culture. Built through collaboration. REDESIGN AFRICA. The Night Africa Wore Her Crown The Legacy Gala & Awards night brought together more than 1,000 distinguished guests, representing an extraordinary convergence of business, government, entertainment, culture and society. Among the dignitaries were Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu , Deputy Governor Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat , prominent business leaders, industry executives, celebrities and long-standing friends of the institution. It was a gathering that reflected not simply the prestige of a hotel, but the depth of relationships cultivated across generations. The evening’s entertainment brought together internationally celebrated musician Wyclef Jean and Nigerian highlife sensation Flavour , creating a memorable meeting of African and Caribbean musical heritage. Music, fashion, theatrical expression and celebration converged in a spectacle befitting the occasion. Yet, beyond the performances lay a more compelling message. African creativity is not a decorative addition to hospitality. It is one of it’s greatest competitive advantages. Africa’s music travels the world, African fashion influences global runways, African cuisine carries the memory of generations, African storytelling continues to captivate audiences far beyond our borders and, many started on Eko Hotels grounds. The question is no longer whether Africa possesses what the world desires, t he question is whether we are sufficiently intentional about converting these cultural assets into sustainable industries, jobs, investments and compelling destination experiences. At The Gala, Eko Hotels offered its own answer. Africa need not borrow another continent’s identity to earn the world’s admiration. She need only invest boldly enough in her own. There is, however, another story that deserves equal billing. It is the story of the people, n ot the famous faces photographed beneath the lights, n ot the glittering personalities whose arrival commands applause b ut the extraordinary men and women whose daily dedication has sustained Eko Hotels for half a century. These are the custodians of the brand. The quiet architects of its reputation and t he human infrastructure behind its commercial success. For fifty years, generations of employees have given their skills, energy, creativity and commitment to an institution that has become part of Nigeria’s hospitality heritage. Their stories may not always appear in annual reports, but their fingerprints are everywhere. A hotel may be built with concrete, steel and capital. But a legacy is built with people who choose, every day, to care. The Chairman, Christopher Chagoury boldly said in an interview. Perhaps, this is one of the most important lessons of Eko Hotels at fifty: buildings can be replicated, interiors redesigned and technology acquired, but a culture of excellence must be nurtured and that culture is ultimately human. The Leadership understands the weight of the legacy. Behind every enduring institution is a succession of decisions, investments, sacrifices and moments when leadership chooses long-term value over immediate convenience. The golden jubilee provided an opportunity to recognize the vision and stewardship that have guided Eko Hotels through five decades. Under the leadership of their Managing Director, Ghassan Faddoul , General Manager Danny Kioupouroglou and the wider executive management team, the institution continues to strengthen it’s position as a defining hospitality destination. Their collective responsibility extends beyond protecting a celebrated past, to redesigning a future, our past will be proud of, long after we are gone. It is to ensure that the institution remains competitive, innovative and relevant to future generations. item.title: Yinka Ogunbiyi Shows HaloBraid’s Automated Hair-Braiding Technology in New Demo
item.description: Harvard graduate Yinka Ogunbiyi, creator of the automated HaloBraid device engineered to complete braids up to five times faster. What if you could get your braids done in a fraction of the usual time and still leave the salon with the style you wanted? A new demonstration of HaloBraid, the automated braiding device created by Nigerian-American engineer and Harvard graduate Yinka Ogunbiyi , gives us a closer look at how that could work. Designed to help professional hairdressers braid hair up to five times faster while reducing the physical strain that comes with hours of styling, HaloBraid is now being demonstrated in action. And the interesting part is that the machine doesn’t do everything. The stylist still plays an important role in the process. Here’s how it works. The stylist sections the hair, applies the necessary products and starts the braid by hand before feeding it into the device. HaloBraid then handles the repetitive weaving along the length of the hair, while the stylist returns to finish and seal the ends. This means the machine takes care of a time-consuming part of the process, with the stylist still responsible for creating the final hairstyle. For Yinka, the idea behind HaloBraid comes from a very personal experience. Sharing the story behind the invention, she said: My braid story starts at age four, sitting between my mum’s legs as she braided my hair for the first time. Since then, I’ve spent thousands of hours getting my hair braided — and heard the same story from stylists and clients again and again: braiding is beautiful, but it takes too much time and too much strain. As a biomechanical engineer, I knew there had to be a better way, so we built HaloBraid with stylists from the beginning, bringing together inventors, designers, and builders behind some of the world’s most loved hair and beauty products. HaloBraid was built for my mum, my stylists, my aunties, and people around the world who know what it means to spend hours in the chair. The company has also secured $7 million in seed funding, with the investment round led by Seven Seven Six, the venture capital firm founded by Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian , who is married to tennis champion Serena Williams . With the newly shared demonstration, HaloBraid is showing how its technology works alongside professional stylists, combining hand-braiding techniques with automated weaving to reduce the time and physical effort involved in protective hairstyling. Artificial intelligence is changing how people learn, work, build businesses and access information. Photo by Jean Biziman for Gates Foundation One area, and perhaps the most important area, where this cooperation matters is language. There are thousands of languages spoken in Africa. But much of the technology used to develop AI relies on data in widely spoken languages (in many cases in Africa, English and French), leaving many African languages underrepresented. This limits who can use these tools and how useful they can be. For a young person who speaks an African language but struggles with English or French, AI may not offer the same opportunities it offers someone who is fluent in these languages. The Masakhane research community is working to address this problem by developing natural language processing technologies for African languages. The community consists of Africans representing different languages across Africa. It is an example of what can happen when African researchers collaborate to make technology more inclusive. Through initiatives such as the Masakhane AI Languages Hub, researchers can develop datasets across 40 African languages to support the creation of more useful AI tools. In the 2026 Goalkeepers Report , Bill Gates said AI must b e able to work in every language spoken to create significant equality. Goalkeepers 2026 Report African countries can build on this work by investing in shared language resources, supporting local researchers and making datasets available for responsible use. Instead of each country working independently on similar challenges, regional partnerships could help researchers share knowledge and develop tools that serve communities across borders. This could make it easier for young Africans to access educational resources, health information and other services in languages they understand. AI can also help make opportunities available to people outside major cities. In agriculture, for example, PlantVillage Nuru uses a smartphone camera and AI to help farmers identify crop diseases. The application can work offline, making it useful in areas where internet connectivity is limited. Although the tool does not remove every challenge farmers face, it demonstrates how AI can make certain kinds of technical knowledge more accessible. Solutions like this could benefit young farmers and agricultural entrepreneurs across Africa. Countries facing similar agricultural problems could collaborate to test, adapt and improve existing tools instead of developing separate solutions from the beginning. Universities, research institutions and governments could support these efforts by sharing expertise and investing in technologies that respond to local conditions. African countries can work together to create more opportunities for young people to learn AI skills, participate in research, access mentorship and build businesses. Regional programmes could connect students with employers and investors across borders, allowing talent to find opportunities beyond national job markets. They could also help young people learn from one another and develop solutions that can be adapted to different African communities. Bill Gates in Rwanda. Photo by Jean Biziman for Gates Foundation. These efforts must be supported by investments in electricity, affordable internet, devices and digital education. Without these basics, AI training and other opportunities may continue to reach those who already have the most access. Governments and technology companies must also protect users’ data, address bias and ensure that the development of AI does not exclude women, people with disabilities or young people in rural communities. The African Union’s Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy , endorsed in 2024, provides a basis for countries to pursue a more coordinated approach to AI development. The challenge now is to translate that ambition into practical opportunities for young people. Africa does not have to approach every AI challenge as a separate national problem. By sharing knowledge, supporting local innovation and opening more pathways to education and employment, countries can make their investments go further. Success should not be measured only by the number of AI tools developed or the amount of money invested in the technology. It should also be measured by whether a young person, regardless of where they live, has a fair chance to use AI to improve their life. This will be part of the conversation centred around this year’s Goalkeepers 2026 . item.title: Taiwo Awoniyi Honoured with ‘Beyond the Pitch’ Award at the 2026 Best of Africa Awards in London
item.description: Taiwo Awoniyi posing on the red carpet at the Best of Africa Awards 2026 in London. Nigerian international striker Taiwo Awoniyi has picked up the prestigious ‘Beyond the Pitch’ Award at the 2026 Best of Africa Awards in London, marking a major moment of recognition for his work both on and off the football field. Known for his clinical goalscoring ability and strength upfront, the Nottingham Forest and Super Eagles forward plays as a central striker at the highest level of European football. Beyond his professional career in the English Premier League, Taiwo has consistently directed his resources towards community development, healthcare support, and youth empowerment in Nigeria—most notably through his funding and sponsorship of the Kwara Kiddies League, an initiative providing structured grassroots football opportunities for young talents in Kwara State. The Best of Africa Awards, held annually in London, celebrate the outstanding contributions of African figures and individuals of African heritage across sports, entertainment, and social impact. Supported by the Professional Footballers’ Association (PFA), the ‘Beyond the Pitch’ accolade specifically highlights athletes who use their global platform to drive tangible social change and uplift their home communities. Taking to Instagram to reflect on the honour, Taiwo shared a message with his followers: Life can give you so much, but what truly matters is what you choose to do with what you’ve been given. Grateful to receive the PFA Beyond the Pitch Award at the Best of Africa Awards 2026. His philanthropic commitments include fully funding the annual Kwara Kiddies League tournament, providing kits, equipment, and cash prizes for grassroots teams across Ilorin and surrounding areas to help young footballers build sustainable career pathways. item.title: A City of Cities: Heineken Celebrates Lagos’ Culture and Style At Heineken Lagos Fashion Week 2026
item.description: Heineken returns to Lagos Fashion Week from October 29 to 31, 2026, continuing a decade-long partnership that has evolved beyond sponsorship into a platform for creative collaboration, cultural expression and shared experiences. Through City of Cities: Where Taste Rules , Heineken will celebrate the people, cultures and creative expressions shaping Lagos, bringing its presence to life across the Heineken Lounge, Heineken Runway Showcase, Heineken Studio and the After Party. First introduced in Lagos in 2025, City of Cities: Where Taste Rules celebrates the diversity that defines the city, where different cultures, styles, communities and perspectives converge. From fashion and music to food, art and social experiences, Lagos draws its character from the people and influences that shape it. For Heineken, this reflects the many ways taste is expressed, experienced and shared. Over the past decade, Heineken’s partnership with Lagos Fashion Week has evolved through initiatives that explore the relationship between fashion, craftsmanship and taste. From the sustainable fashion focus of Woven Threads in 2022 and the Dyelab collaboration in 2023 to the H45 Collection in 2024 and the introduction of City of Cities: Where Taste Rules in 2025, each chapter has offered a distinct expression of the partnership. In 2026, Heineken continues this legacy, creating new opportunities to connect with the people, ideas and experiences shaping contemporary Nigerian fashion and culture. This year’s Heineken Lagos Fashion Week theme, CRAFTED , provides a natural context for this next chapter, celebrating intentionality, artistry, craftsmanship and more considered approaches to fashion and sustainability. Reflecting this spirit, Heineken will bring its presence to life across the week through the Heineken Lounge, the Cruise Collection runway, Heineken Studio and the Heineken Studio After Party, creating experiences that extend beyond the runway. Making its Nigerian debut, Heineken Studio introduces a new dimension to the brand’s exploration of taste and innovation. Described as Heineken’s Playground of Innovation, Studio explores new ways to serve and experience lager through experimentation, brewer expertise and discovery. item.title: Tiwa Savage Is Giving Rock-Chic Glamour in Black Latex and Purple Fur
item.description: Tiwa Savage posing in a royal purple fur coat layered over a black latex catsuit. A glossy black catsuit and a purple fur coat? Tiwa Savage says she knows how to make both work, and work perfectly! And looking at her latest outfit, we have absolutely no reason to argue. The Afrobeats superstar stepped out in a figure-hugging black latex catsuit with a plunging V-neckline, throwing a plush, oversized royal purple fur coat over the look. Because when you’re Tiwa Savage, why settle for one fashion statement when you can make two? And can we talk about the accessories? Chunky gold bangles stacked on her wrists, sculptural gold earrings and a razor-sharp black bob that gave the entire look an extra dose of attitude. Between the glossy latex, the rich purple fur and those bold gold pieces, Tiwa had every detail working in her favour. Tiwa Savage styling a black latex catsuit with a royal purple fur coat and gold hardware. Now, here’s something to borrow from Tiwa’s style book. A fitted catsuit already does a lot for your silhouette, so pairing it with an oversized coat gives the outfit a completely different shape. That contrast between something sleek and something voluminous is what makes the combination so interesting. And rather than reaching for barely-there jewellery, take Tiwa’s approach with chunky metallic pieces that can hold their own against the outfit. Tiwa Savage backstage wearing a black latex catsuit and gold earrings There’s also a little colour lesson here. Black and purple make a gorgeous pairing, particularly when you play around with textures. The shine of the latex against the softness of the fur makes both colours look even richer, while the gold accessories add warmth to the overall look. So, the next time you’re putting together an all-black outfit and wondering what could give it a little extra personality, you might want to take a page out of Tiwa Savage’s book. item.title: Cynthia Erivo & Ayoade Bamgboye Take “Wicked” to LagOz in Hilarious SNL UK Sketch
item.description: Cynthia Erivo and Ayoade Bamgboye posing through traditional beaded door curtains on the set of Nigerian Wicked. If you thought you’d seen every possible spin on Wicked, think again. West End and Broadway royalty Cynthia Erivo recently stepped onto the Saturday Night Live UK (SNL UK) stage to deliver a masterclass in comedy—teaming up with Ayoade Bamgboye to reimagine the magical land of Oz as a chaotic, low-budget Nollywood blockbuster. Titled “ Nigerian Wicked “ and presented by the fictional Holy Ghost Productions (the satirical masterminds behind classic titles like Beyonce’s Revenge and Light Skin, Dark Heart ), the viral sketch is a love letter to Nollywood tropes complete with a gloriously stressful sound mix. In this universe , Elphaba (played with maximum green-paint intensity by Ayoade Bamgboye) and Glinda (brought to life by Cynthia Erivo in a pink tracksuit, blonde wig, and matching cap) are sharing a room stacked with vintage trunk luggage. Their relationship is wonderfully tense , highlighted by an unforgettable moment where Glinda casually slaps Elphaba because she is “very classless” , only for Elphaba to complain that the room smells like egg. Ayoade Bamgboye as Elphaba and Cynthia Erivo as Glinda sitting on set during the Nigerian Wicked sketch on Saturday Night Live UK. Things get even wilder when the duo boards a train to the land of LagOz to see The Wizard (played by Hammed Animashaun ) , who turns out to be completely broke, rocking a “No-lex” watch instead of a Rolex, and offering his guests some off Bailey’s Irish Cream. While Elphaba is simply hoping her magical transformation defies gravity and earns her a “skinny BBL”, Glinda is laser-focused on her ultimate priority: getting her hands on a Birkin bag. Complete with flying monkeys , Professor Goat , dramatic musical interludes , and a full, gloriously long credit sequence introducing Cynthia by her full traditional name— Cynthia Onyedinmanasu Chinasaokwu Owezuke Amarachukwu Echeumuna Erivo ——this sketch is pure comedic gold from start to finish.
